A distribution assigns probabilities or densities to possible data; a likelihood evaluates the observed data as a function of model parameters.
Maximum likelihood and maximum a posteriori estimation use that likelihood to choose one parameter value, with different treatment of prior information.
The practical question is which parameter setting best accounts for the observations within the chosen model family; the optimisation does not itself establish that the family describes reality.

## Likelihood and maximum likelihood {#estimation}

For fixed observations $\mathcal D=\{x_i\}_{i=1}^n$ and an [independent-sample]{.term key="independent-samples"} model, the likelihood is

$$
  \mathcal L(\theta;\mathcal D)=\prod_{i=1}^n p_\theta(x_i).
$$

It is a function of parameters, not a normalised probability distribution over parameters.
Maximum likelihood estimation chooses parameters maximising this function, equivalently minimising the negative log-likelihood.
For classification, that gives empirical [cross-entropy](entropy.qmd#cross-entropy), as derived below.

## Classification likelihood {#classification}

For classification, the likelihood is the probability assigned to the fixed observed labels, viewed as a function of the model parameters $w$, with the inputs held fixed.
Changing $w$ changes the probabilities assigned to those labels.
The likelihood is not a probability distribution over the parameters.

Suppose the labels are conditionally independent under the model, given the inputs and parameters.
Then the likelihood of the observed labels is the product of their predicted probabilities.
Maximizing this likelihood is equivalent to minimizing the sum of their cross-entropy losses:

$$
  \begin{gathered}
  \text{maximize likelihood}\\
  \Updownarrow\\
  \text{minimize negative log-likelihood}.
  \end{gathered}
$$

For a fixed dataset of $n\geq1$ examples, dividing this sum by $n$ gives the empirical mean loss without changing its minimizers.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: from likelihood to mean cross-entropy"}

Let $q_i(w)$ be the positive probability the model assigns to the observed class for example $i$.
Under the conditional independence assumption, the likelihood is

$$
  \mathcal L(w)=\prod_{i=1}^{n}q_i(w).
$$

The logarithm is strictly increasing, so it preserves which parameters maximize the likelihood and turns the product into a sum:

$$
  \ln\mathcal L(w)
  =\ln\!\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}q_i(w)\right)
  =\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln q_i(w).
$$

Negating this expression turns maximization into minimization:

$$
  -\ln\mathcal L(w)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}-\ln q_i(w).
$$

For a binary target $y_i\in\{0,1\}$, let $p_i(w)$ be the predicted probability of class $1$.
The probability of the observed class can be written as

$$
  q_i(w)=p_i(w)^{y_i}\left(1-p_i(w)\right)^{1-y_i}.
$$

Its negative logarithm is binary cross-entropy:

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  &-\ln q_i(w)\\
  &\quad =-y_i\ln p_i(w)\\
  &\qquad -(1-y_i)\ln\left(1-p_i(w)\right).
  \end{aligned}
$$

For a categorical target, the same term is $-\ln p_{i,\text{observed class}}(w)$.
The empirical mean cross-entropy is therefore

$$
  L(w)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}-\ln q_i(w)
  =-\frac{1}{n}\ln\mathcal L(w).
$$

The factor $1/n$ is a positive constant, so it does not change the minimizers.

:::

## Maximum a posteriori estimation {#map-estimation}

Return to the notation $\mathcal D=\{x_i\}_{i=1}^n$ and $\mathcal L(\theta;\mathcal D)$ for the fixed dataset and its likelihood.
Maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation specifies a [prior]{.term key="prior"} density or mass function $p(\theta)$.
The [posterior]{.term key="posterior"} satisfies $p(\theta\mid\mathcal D)\propto\mathcal L(\theta;\mathcal D)p(\theta)$.
Assume the observations are independent under the model for a fixed $\theta$, so the likelihood is $\prod_i p_\theta(x_i)$.
MAP then minimises the negative log posterior up to a constant:

$$
  -\sum_i\ln p_\theta(x_i)-\ln p(\theta).
$$

For example, a zero-mean isotropic Gaussian parameter prior contributes a squared parameter penalty.
A MAP point estimate is not the full posterior and does not retain all its uncertainty.

## A Bernoulli estimate and its interpretation {#example}

Suppose four independent trials share one success probability $\theta$, and the observed sequence has three successes and one failure.
The sequence likelihood is $\mathcal L(\theta)=\theta^3(1-\theta)$ for $0\leq\theta\leq1$, and its maximum occurs at $\hat\theta=3/4$.
The estimate is a parameter value selected using the data, while the likelihood is the entire function used to select it.
The estimate alone does not give a probability that the unknown parameter equals $3/4$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Derivation: the Bernoulli maximum-likelihood estimate"}

For $0<\theta<1$, the log-likelihood and derivative are

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  \log\mathcal L(\theta)&=3\log\theta+\log(1-\theta),\\
  \frac{d}{d\theta}\log\mathcal L(\theta)
  &=\frac{3-4\theta}{\theta(1-\theta)}.
  \end{aligned}
$$

The derivative is positive below $3/4$ and negative above it.
Both endpoints give zero likelihood for this mixed success-and-failure sequence, so $3/4$ is its global maximum.

:::

The calculation relies on a shared success probability and independence across trials.
If those assumptions change, the product model and the meaning of its estimate must be reconsidered.
For continuous observations, likelihood factors are densities, so their numerical values need not lie below one and do not represent probabilities of exact observed points.
